subheader: The vanished Horneburg becomes visible again
name: Burginsel Horneburg
about_html:
The Vanished Castle

The castle of Horneburg has vanished – and yet its traces remain to this day. How the complex actually looked before its destruction in 1645, no one knows for certain. There are no paintings, no engravings, and no coins that depict it. For centuries, its appearance remained a mystery.

It was not until recently that the search for the complex resumed. In 2020, the municipality of Horneburg was able to conclude a long-term lease for the Burginsel with the owning family – direct descendants of the former castle lords. This not only achieved an important step towards the restoration of the town center, but also laid the foundation for making the island accessible to visitors and learning more about its history.

Later that same year, the district archaeology of the Stade district examined the Burginsel (main castle) and the outer ward with the most modern geophysical methods. The investigations were conducted in collaboration with the University of Hamburg and the company Eastern Atlas. Classical excavations were hardly possible due to the high groundwater level and massive layers of rubble. All the more surprising were the results: At approximately 1.50 meters depth, the foundation structures of the main castle became clearly visible. For the first time, the size, number, and arrangement of the buildings could be understood. In addition, archaeological finds discovered during metal detector surveys and during archaeological supervision of renovation measures provided clues about life in the castle and its violent destruction.

Research and Reconstruction

Based on these discoveries, castle researchers Menno Mennenga and Joachim Zeune were commissioned to reconstruct the complex. From the archaeological findings, they developed site plans, floor plans, and views of the former buildings. Even possible building materials and different types of houses could be reconstructed. Thus, a scientifically sound picture of the historical complex was created for the first time.

The current design of the Burginsel also incorporates these findings. The landscape architecture office + was inspired by the historical structures when redesigning the park area. Benches mark the former building foundations, fence elements recall the palisade fence that once surrounded the island. Two bridges connect the Burginsel with the town and also make it a special place to stay and hold events.

From the beginning, one idea was central: not just to convey history, but to make it tangible. In collaboration with Prof. Thomas P. Kersten and his team from the HafenCity University Hamburg, the research results were digitally reconstructed and translated into virtual worlds.

Experience History

Today, visitors can discover the historical complex in two different ways:

The AR version ('Augmented Reality') projects the former complex directly onto the Burginsel in the real environment and makes it tangible on-site with a smartphone or tablet. The VR version ('Virtual Reality') additionally enables a virtual tour in three-dimensional representation.

The VR version can be experienced at the Handwerksmuseum of the Samtgemeinde Horneburg with a VR headset. The AR version is available directly on this website.
history: Where today only a silent island lies, once stood an important castle complex.
history_text: For centuries, the Horneburg was the scene of power struggles, feuds, and changing rulers – and the origin of today's municipality of Horneburg.
history_more: Read more about the history of the castle
history_fulltext:
Founding and Strategic Importance

The medieval Horneburg was built as a water castle in a politically and militarily significant border region. Here, the areas of influence of the Archbishopric of Bremen, the Diocese of Verden, and the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg met. The castle controlled an important traffic junction: on the one hand, the Lühe coming from the Elbe, through which the Alte Land could be reached, on the other hand, an important land route from Stade to Buxtehude and Harburg – today's B 73 – crossed the river.

The castle was built in 1255 by the Archbishop of Bremen in response to the expansion of Harburg by the Welf dukes. The garrison consisted of Bremen cathedral ministériales who were enfeoffed in the surrounding area of the castle on the Geest and in the Alte Land. They were initially firmly bound to the Harsefeld monastery via castle fiefs.

Power Center of the Castle Men

With the founding of the city of Buxtehude, the castle lost some of its original border function, but it developed into an independent center of power of the castle men. These gradually transformed fiefs into communal property. A closely connected castle community emerged, held together by mutual protection and loyalty alliances.

In the early 14th century, the Horneburg fell into several major conflicts. Particularly famous was the flight of Knight Heinrich von Borch, the so-called 'Isern Hinnerk', to the castle. After the conquest of his ancestral castle, he sought refuge here in 1311, but was taken prisoner after a siege by allied troops of the Archbishop of Bremen, the Duke of Lüneburg, and the Bishop of Verden. The castle men were temporarily expelled, but returned later. In the following decades, the Horneburg was repeatedly the starting point for armed feuds and raids, which solidified its reputation as a robber baron's nest.

In the 15th century, too, the complex remained the scene of regional power struggles. A siege in 1426 failed, but led to the so-called Horneburg Feud. The castle men subsequently undertook numerous raids into neighboring territories. Only with the so-called Urfehde of 1443 did the situation gradually calm down. Nevertheless, the castle remained a political security risk.

Destruction and Change

At the beginning of the 16th century, the castle men increasingly left the outer ward and built new noble seats in the surrounding area. During the Thirty Years' War, the Horneburg changed hands several times and was ultimately destroyed by warfare. After Swedish troops captured the complex in 1645, Hans Christoph von Königsmarck had the by then militarily obsolete fortress demolished. On parts of the former outer ward, the Gut Horneburg I, the so-called castle, was later built.

The Complex and Its Surroundings

The Horneburg was built as a water castle in the swampy lowlands of the Lühe. The approximately 85 x 75 meter wide, nearly round main castle was completely surrounded by a moat, which was fed by arms of the Lühe. Palisades protected the complex. On the outer ward were farm buildings and the courtyards of the castle men.

The castle was connected to the surrounding area by several dams. Along these paths, craftsmen and merchants settled – the origin of today's town of Horneburg.

How the Horneburg originally looked can only be partially understood today. Since neither contemporary depictions nor detailed descriptions have survived, today's knowledge is based primarily on archaeological investigations and finds. They provide insights into the complex, life in the castle, and its destruction – but many questions remain unanswered.

ar_overlay_header: How to use the AR feature
ar_overlay_instruction_1: Move your device slowly so the castle appears in your camera.
ar_overlay_instruction_2: Explore the island and discover the complex from different perspectives.
ar_overlay_instruction_3: Tap on the buildings to learn more about them.
ar_overlay_instruction_4: If something doesn't work, use the reload button.
